The top of the page is 275. My first question, Mr. Stojkic, is that the book you have in your hands, are you familiar with that book? Can you tell us what this is, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: This is the logbook which was kept by the duty officer at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have access to this book and did you write anything in this book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at the entry where it says, at the left side of the page, entry number 8, for 13 July. I will read the entry in English and you can read it in the original in your own language. Where it says, "I took over duty on schedule from Lieutenant Drago Nikolic at 2300 hours." Bearing in mind your response to my colleague earlier, what do you make of this entry in the book, Mr. Stojkic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer you now, down on the same page, on the 14th of July 1995, and I'd like to read the second paragraph, and you can look in your own language, where it says, "Enemy forces are very active over the communication lines and are preparing to attack our forces." Do you see this paragraph in the original book in your own language?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question, based on this paragraph, is: Is this the kind of information which could be obtained by the duty officer at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, one thing that should read here is who he received the information from. And there is no way he could have learned that at the IKM, as far as the equipment at the IKM is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain that a little more for the benefit of the Trial Chamber? Why is it that based on the equipment at the IKM, he cannot obtain this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: If this was communicated from the brigade command, then it should be noted here who it was who sent that message to the IKM. And since there is no interception centre at the IKM, there is no way he could have obtained this information over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you were working at the IKM where did you get information from and what did you do with that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Every information that we received from the battalion, or from the brigade command, we would enter into our daily notebook of the duty signalsman on duty and then we would hand that over to the office at the IKM. Now, what he wrote in his logbook on the basis of our notebook I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what kind of information would the battalions give to you? What were you looking for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: At 1600 hours, we would carry a checkout, as to the situation in the battalion, whether they went into action, whether there were any killed or wounded or things like that and then we would hand that over first of all to the officer on duty at the forward command post and when we had collected all the information up from all the battalions, we would send it to the head office, to the brigade and the signalsman on duty who would then take it to the officer on duty who was the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Let me just clarify a few parts of the answer you just gave. Would I be right to say then that the information would be collected at the IKM and transmitted to the brigade? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you called the brigade, yourself, in order to -- did you speak to the duty officer yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: You mean the operative?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, did you speak to the operations duty officer at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. The witness has said this material got reported to the duty officer at the IKM and now Mr. Bourgon is switching that to the duty officer at the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once again, I'm not going to say anything but my colleague, but his objection is ill founded. If you read, Mr. President, the answer of the witness, and I read from page 7 now, line 17 to 23, this is not what the witness said. So my colleague is not -- his objection is not founded, and I'm actually trying to clarify this and where he says that it was then taken to the officer on duty who was the commander of the brigade, that was my next question now, to clarify what the witness meant by that. If I can just freeze.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Please answer the question, Mr. Stojkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So Mr. Stojkic, when this information, as you say, had been collected from all the battalions, you mention we would send it to the head office, to the brigade, and the signalsman on duty. That was your answer. I just wanted to know, did you yourself speak to the duty officer at the brigade or did you speak only to the signalsman on duty there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Only to the duty signalsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you say that it would then -- he would then take it to the officer on duty, who was the commander of the brigade, were those -- is that what you said or do you wish to clarify this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: The signalsman at the switchboard would write this report of ours from the IKM and then take it to the duty operative and then the duty operative would take it to the commander of the brigade or the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you another entry. But this time in a different exhibit. And that is at the notebook of the brigade operations duty officer, that is P377. Now I would also ask if we could show the witness the original book, please. And if I can have in English on e-court, page 13? The page I would like to show the witness in the original book is ERN 5737. So, Mr. Stojkic, I'm sorry, the page I'd like you to look at, if you'd look at the top of the original, is 5748. And in e-court, it is English page 24. Do you have the original book with page 5748?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On e-court, we do not have that. We have 5790. And I was looking for 5748. According to my records, it should be English page 24. If I can have e-court in English, please? We have the B/C/S on the e-court. Okay. Which page do you now have, Mr. Stojkic, before you in your language, in the original book, at the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness did say 5748 but the 4 is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The important thing is that we have got the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the witness has the right page before him. Now we are just looking for the page in English and it should be 377, page 24 in English. Well, I have the B/C/S here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have the English. I just want to make sure that it is the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you can look, Mr. Stojkic, at the top of that page, can you read the entry there, even though it's handwritten and might be difficult to read, can you tell us what it says at the top of the page there? 5748, right at the top.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: "The security person of the IKM, behind the back of Krizanic there is shooting, Potocari, individual shooting" I can't understand what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what do you make, Mr. Stojkic, of that entry where it says "the security person at the IKM"? What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: That he was on duty at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: From security. It could be Trbic, Petkovic, possibly Nikolic was sent back. Had there been somebody else, it would say duty officer, not bezbednjak [phoen], security person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So is there any possibility that on that day, that this was Galic who was at the IKM at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is superspeculative. Possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. President, I fail to see the purpose of the objection. The witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are fine with the question. But the witness must, of course, know and make sure that in answering it, he doesn't speculate. He either knows or he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll say the question over again, Mr. Stojkic. You mentioned that this had to be a security person. Was Mr. Galic a security person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned in response to a question by my colleague that Galic was never on duty at the IKM while you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you saw -- did you ever see Galic at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court when that was and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I would see Galic at the forward command post when the higher-ranking officers would come by. He was escorting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Stojkic, having a conversation with Galic about the fact that whether or not he was at the IKM on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain when that conversation took place, to the best of your knowledge, and what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Near my house, there is a car wash service. And that's where we met. He started the conversation for the 13th of July 1995, and he was convincing me, how come I didn't remember that we had spent the duty hours together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was your answer to that question? Or what happened during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I told him, "I'm sorry, you're an older man but you're lying."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions, Mr. Stojkic, concerning the -- some technical questions about the duty at the IKM. Can you explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the exact procedure when you would call either -- well, let's begin with the brigade command. When you call the brigade command, how do you do it? How does that take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I just dial the number of the switchboard and get through to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who answers at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: The telephonist manning the switchboard who is on duty at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is it possible to bypass the switchboard and call directly to the duty officer, for example?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: We always had to go through the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you wanted to call a battalion from the IKM, how would that take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: The same thing: Through the switchboard in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what would the switchboard in the barracks do if you wanted to speak, for example, to 4 Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: It would link us up to the IKM, establish communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what about the duty officer? Could he call the IKM? I'm talking about the brigade operative duty officer. Could he call the IKM?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: The duty officer at the IKM? Is that what you mean? To call up the brigade commander, is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll make that clear. I'm sorry, my question was not clear enough. If the brigade operative duty officer, at the brigade command, can he call the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How does he do it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: The same thing, via the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we mentioned a little earlier the existence of a trench close to the IKM. Can you tell us where exactly this trench was? Physically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: The trench was, looking at it from the forward command post, where the three-barrel pieces were, well, to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was the purpose, if you know, of this trench?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: It was an observation post for the high-ranking officers when they came to visit and tour the area. So that they could supervise the line, have a view of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to your recollection, was there a field phone between the trench and the IKM itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if there was a senior officer present at the -- in the trench, he could speak to the IKM? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before their arrival, one of us signalsman would go and establish contact with the forward command post so that it was already operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there was also a -- correct me if I'm wrong -- an RUP 12 radio at the IKM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you use that a lot, that radio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When would you use the radio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: We would only use the radio if the line communication was down, or wire communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, using that -- your normal means of communication with the brigade command or the battalions, I take it, then, would be the field phone or the inductor line, as you might call them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall if codes were used at all when you spoke on that telephone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody else had an opportunity? Was that a procedure that was used when somebody at the forward command post would speak to somebody at the brigade command, were codes used in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Codes were never used from the forward command post to the brigade command, while I was on duty. I can't speak for my other colleagues. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at the duty officers who were present at the IKM or those who did regular shifts, to the best of your recollections, who were those officers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic, Milorad Trbic, Sreten Milosevic, Mijo Dragutinovic. Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you develop any relationship with any of these officers? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I was on good terms with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I could have a quick minute, Mr. President, I would just like to check my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just two questions more, Mr. President, and I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The first question, Mr. Stojkic is regarding the book you referred to, talking about not the duty officer's book at the IKM but the book that was -- the one that you were responsible for or the communicator's book. Did you ever see this book again after July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall when the IKM was -- until when the IKM was operational?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, after the Muslims passed through, the IKM was closed two or three months later, was shut down two or three months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would just like you to show you one more entry in the book that you have before you now, that is 377. I would just like to show you one further entry, and the top of the page would be 5741. In English, it is page 17 for e-court, please. Do you have this page, Mr. Stojkic, with 5741? And I refer you -- there appears to be a name written there in block letters, name is Jerkic. I refer you to the entry just above that. Can you tell us what this entry reads?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: You mean the square there? The rectangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not the square. Just to the left where it starts with 16 dot or dash 0.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: "Two states regular, Palma 2, situation regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. That's the entry?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, they don't have the English once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was checking out the battalion or rather the battalion checking out so see that there was no activity going on and that everything was regular, that the situation was regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So considering that this is the brigade duty operative officer, making this observation, where would this information come from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, it comes from the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How do you know that? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, we from the IKM sent it to the brigade, so it was conveyed by the duty officer to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to know because it doesn't say anything about IKM here. It says "16, Palma 2, situation normal." How do you know it's from the IKM?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Because we were Palma 2. The IKM, that's what it was called, Palma 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at the top of that page, I'm not sure you have it in the original, but I'll simply suggest to you that this is -- took place at 13 -- on the 13th of July, and if you take this entry on the 13th of July, who sent that information to the brigade command, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: The signalsman on duty at the IKM handed over the report to the officer on duty at the IKM, and when he transcribed it into his duty book or logbook, then he says, "Report that to the command that the situation is normal." If there is anything that is not, then that is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And finally, in terms of the qualifications that you had as a signalman, who were the best trained signalmen in the brigade, were those working at the brigade or those working at the battalions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, the brigade signalsmen were better trained than the battalion signalsmen. They were privy to more functions and they were more familiar with a higher number of different pieces of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you yourself, Mr. Stojkic, in more -- especially in 1995, but at any time during the war, did you ever have any disciplinary or legal proceedings instituted against you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I suggest to you that you were a good communicator and a good soldier, always on time, would that correspond to what you were in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Of course, I was a good soldier, never late, always -- everything on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey? Unless you prefer to have the break now. I mean it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can go for what, 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think -- I hope I should finish this witness by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then shall we send the other witness home?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't think I would get put on the spot like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can imagine how uncomfortable people feel when they are left waiting in a room in this environment with no proper air circulation for long hours. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. First I want to show you a document, it's 65 ter 318. This is a document that's in evidence. And it will come up on your screen in B/C/S. This is a document that's called the establishment of tactical group, the 1st Zvornik Brigade for carrying out active combat operations in the Drina Corps. Preparation order. And we want to go down to the section --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As far as I see, this document is not on the list of documents disclosed to us before cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a revised list, and I think it is on -- yeah. Can you confirm that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's on the revised list. It's a result of his testimony that I'm responding to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't he see the revised list, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we want to go down in the B/C/S to the section on 2.1, and 2.1b, just as a brief description of communications squad and it says, "Four soldiers signalmen from the communications company." Do you see that there and --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: There are none here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, go to 2.1b. And it's not a list of names, it just says, "Four soldiers, signalsmen from the communications company"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that fit your recollection, was there four signalsmen that were originally assigned to go down to Srebrenica with this tactical group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: If I could see the names? That would jog my memory, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, so you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I remember some names but I'm not sure that I would be able to guess all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just like, this is not the type of document that would have been accessible to this witness so at least my colleague should lay the context and ask a question as to what he means by what communication resources were sent to the Srebrenica operation. I have no problems with that. But this document is not a document that would have been accessible to this soldier at his level. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All I asked him was does he remember if it was four soldiers and I helped him show the document. He says he can't remember, his memory is not very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's see if we can help your memory. Let's go to 65 ter 3396. And let me give you a hard copy, apparently this electronic version that we have doesn't come up very well and if we could put that on the ELMO. And we can -- if we start, we see that commander Vinko Pandurevic, deputy commander, Milan Jolovic, is that correct, that information so far, from your memory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go down to the communications squad which is the last third of the page. There we go. It says squad commander, private Goran Lakic, and then there is four radio operators, a communications equipment technician, and a radio operator. And we see Dragan Stojkic on that. Are you the Dragan Stojkic that we see on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are those the communication guys you went to Srebrenica with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Timko, Grozdan Savic and Slavisa Jeremic and down there is Yugoslav and as for Trsunovic, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you go to the Zepa operation with them as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said you spent the night at -- near Crna Rijeka, when you went towards Zepa. What did you do the next morning at the Crna Rijeka area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, we were equipped, and we set out for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you -- can you tell us -- this is a historic event. Can you tell us as much as you can remember about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing. We went on foot towards Zepa. At the moment when we arrived, close to their lines, we were deployed and embarked on taking the territory from them up to that evening, and that evening we stopped at the point that was the furthest into the area that we managed to take by then from them. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you in a combat unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Up at the front line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the action, if any? Was there shooting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what unit were you with besides your communication person? Who else was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I was not with my colleagues. That company was short of signalsmen, so I was in Grbovac company but we were in contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this was the Zvornik Brigade company you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was it commanded by that day, the Zvornik Brigade forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Commander Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see him up there on the front lines with you, taking part in the action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: When we were deployed in the direction of Zepa was the last when I saw him. I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you see him when you were going towards Zepa, fighting the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: When we passed Crna Rijeka, maybe a few kilometres after that, and from then on, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this in the action or was this in the transportation? I can't tell from what you meant.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The action itself had not started yet at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you saw him on -- in somewhere near Crna Rijeka before the action that started the next morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Not the following morning but that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you see Vinko Pandurevic the day before the combat started or the day the combat started in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Both the day before and on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You think it's possible you got your dates mixed up a little bit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you get the 13th from? How do you know it was the 13th? This was almost 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember it well. We took Srebrenica on the 11th. On the 12th we went to Crna Rijeka. And -- actually on the 11th we were in Crna Rijeka in the evening. On the 12th we set out and my company returned on the 13th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, it might be a good time to take a break but not much longer, Mr. President. I won't have too much more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now for 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we have a note or a summary from the Defence that tells us that you said that you were quite certain that Mihajlo Galic had never been a duty officer at the IKM. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Not on my shift. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you hear that he was a duty officer on other shifts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No, none of my colleagues ever told me that, nor did I inquire about who the duty officers were actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't really know -- you can't really tell us reliably whether he was or was not a duty officer at sometimes at the IKM in July and August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: As I have told you, not on my shift. And I really wouldn't be able to speak for any of the other colleagues. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you given a chance to review the duty officer forward command notebook prior to giving your account that you were there on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through that just briefly to see if it can help us with this issue. It is 65 ter 935, and we will give you that original book again. And we should start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's just we have a different number from the one I used. I thought that was a P number and now we are using a 65 ter number. Is that an introduced exhibit or a new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's our 65 ter number. It's the number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same number, same book. There is a revised translation. And the B/C/S is -- well, page 130 and the English is page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But if you could, for the book you have, go to what is the ERN last four numbers are 0275 and take him to that ERN number. And we will just wait for the English to come up, and if we can -- B/C/S page 8 for others but if we could bring that up so we see the 13th and the 14th, we can -- okay. This is what you've already looked at that you said was not true. So -- but we can see that Mr. Galic's name is written there on the 13th. And then if we go to the 15th, the next page for both, we can see that, again, in Cyrillic, it's written, well, the English isn't up there yet and I apologise, the English translation has got its -- oh, the actual where the lines are -- there is a slight mix-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to have the original put on the ELMO, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we are okay. But you may notice that there are some things about the English translation that don't match precisely the original and that's something that we'll work on so it matches a better mirror image of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But on e-court, we have -- I don't know where the difference is. I don't know. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are okay so far, the difference changes a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see there again, Major Galic is written, and then we see a signature. Do you recognise that signature, that sort of vertical signature, as saying "Mihajlo Galic"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then let's keep going. Let's go to the next page. It's 0277 in your book. I think you just switch it over for -- now we switch to 22 July. And English should be ERN 2682. Yeah. Okay. And again, in the -- in the far right, we see printed, "Major Mihajlo Galic" and then his signature for 22 July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you recall if you were there on 22 July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that he -- the times start off, I believe, it's 0900, works its way through the afternoon, and then ends at 0730 which would be or should be the next day, on the 23rd, so he would have spent the night if that's correct, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: That's how it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise Mr. Galic's signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you recognise Drago Nikolic's signature, do you think?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I believe I could, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to the next section. It should be, the B/C/S, 00760298. So do you see that 0298? Can you go to that? And the English is 00962704, what I've got. B/C/S page 31. Okay. We've got it up on -- on the board. And again, can you help us with this? It says, "26 August" this name that's written vertically again, is that printed "Mihajlo Galic" and then signed? English page 29.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: You mean 0289? Is that the page that you're referring me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said, at least the interpretation said 289. I think it should be 298. So it's either a mistake in interpretation or he's got the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah, it's 0298.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She'll help you with that. So is that -- is that printed out "Mihajlo Galic" and then his signature next to it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you doubt these two entries that I've just gone over in this IKM book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: In a handwritten form, yes. Before it was in block letters and now these are miniscule, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt that these entries are genuine, these two entries that we've just gone over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's also speculation. Either he knows or he doesn't know. Was he there on those days? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't agree with you at all. Do answer the question, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not able to remember, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Acimovic, who you've said was a signalsman, when do you recall him being around in relation to when you were around at the IKM after getting back from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: It was later on, once I'd already left, but I wouldn't be able to give you the date when I went to the IKM again. Can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've told us once you got back from Zepa, you went to the IKM, you spent the night there, and then you came back to Standard. During that period that you were at the IKM, did you see Mr. Acimovic, the signals guy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could he have been the other person that was with you on duty after you got back from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No. I said that a signalsman from the battalion had been hired for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you talked to Mr. Acimovic at any time in the last couple of months about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you seen him since being in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you talked to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before coming to The Hague, did you talk to him about anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: We did not even see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you travel to The Hague together?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the forward command post, did a vehicle from the headquarters come by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of car was Drago Nikolic usually in in those days, in July? What was he normally transporting -- transported in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: There were several cars that were -- well, whichever was free. We would take that one and go to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about not you but Drago Nikolic, the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade. Didn't they have a vehicle he usually drove around in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's see a document. It's 65 ter 296, pages 1 to 2 in the B/C/S, and pages 1 to 2 in the English. It's not in that book any more. In fact, we might as well get that book back. And this will come up on your screen so take a look at your screen. This is the front page, I believe the English will come up. This is for a little Opel Rekord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I had no sound on my microphone. My colleague could just ask him whether he's familiar with this type of document before he asks any questions. These are vehicle logs. I'm not sure whether this soldier was ever confronted with this type of document before. So that at least we know where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he's not familiar he'll explain what we are talking about. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want you to see this to see if it helps refresh your recollection as to perhaps -- you know what an Opel Rekord looks like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what it looks like but which one was in the barracks, what type of car, I don't know. I can't remember what kind of Opel it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go over to the next section which shows the little -- the travelling of this particular vehicle. It's page 2. And let's zero in on 13 July, if we can, on both of them. And we can see on this that this vehicle, according to this log, on the 13th, went from Standard to the IKM, to Zvornik, to Loko, to Orahovac, to Zvornik, to Orahovac, and it goes on Standard, Bratunac, Zvornik. Now this clearly had importance to someone to put it in this log. Does this help refresh your recollection if were you there on the 13th when this vehicle came by?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, as far as I see, it is the 8th month, not July. It's 13/8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It looks like that. Mr. McCloskey? At least what we see on the monitor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think he's -- I think that's correct but we can see the other side, that it's speaking of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The title page of the document. We can go to the title page of the document, which is the previous page, 01, 7 through 31, 07.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this particular entry is for the month of August, for 8th month. It is not a question related the first page of document but for some particular entry, for 13th of July and there is no 13th of July, just 13 of -- 13/8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, if we take a close look, it starts off in July and then when it gets to the 7th of July, it switches to August. It's our position that this is a mistake and that it's as we continue to look at the document, we can see it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Of course, that remains without prejudice to the whole argument, whether it's July or August. What we are seeing on the English version also seems to be a little bit different. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is our position that this is obviously a wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but we are leaving that unprejudiced. You don't need to worry about that. Yes, go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. A simple question: This particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to the second page that you were referring the witness to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please, if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, looking at this, and an Opel Rekord, and I think it says, 3, in that column, related to the number of people, so we have now got an Opel Rekord and three people coming by the IKM on the 13th, and it's our position that this is a mistake and it's July. Do you remember anything like that? Does that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: This went by -- had a car gone by in the afternoon, I would have seen it, but that might have been in the morning before I reached the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's slide this over and see if you recognise the signature on the right-hand side for that day. Recognise any -- that -- any of those signatures, those two or three signatures at the end there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could they be Milorad Trbic? You must have seen his signature at some point.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to -- it's the same 65 ter number, it's the same Opel Rekord but a different front page, it's ERN 00694701. Should be page 3 in B/C/S and in English. This one is a little different. It starts from the 14th of July, continues through 31 July like the other one. It's the Opel Rekord with the same number P428, and it starts with the 14th of July. Can we now go to the next page? And I guess we better zero in on that left-hand column as best we can. Starting at the top. Okay. We can see it starts off with a 7 for the 14th, then it gets to an 8th, and they are crossing things out, by the time we get to the 16th, it's getting pretty messy and then by the time we get to the 20th, it gets back to the 7th of July. But just if we again go back to the top, if we could, this is the vehicle that on the 14th goes to various places, including Orahovac. And the next day goes to various places, including Rocevic. And the next day, various places including Kozluk. And the next day, Kula, Pilica, Loko. Could we go over to the far right-hand section of this? Those first -- those signatures right there, who is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that look like Drago Nikolic's signature to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll not re-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can address the Court without the witness hearing because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw you standing. I'm not asking to you ask questions. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I spoke with my client during the recess and there is one question I forgot to ask which is not something that is really contended. With my colleague's permission, the question is simply how long he has known Drago Nikolic for. If my colleague allows it I will ask him the question. If not, then I will not ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I don't think it should depend entirely upon -- on Mr. McCloskey. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkic, I have one more question for you which I've obtained leave from the Trial Chamber to ask you. Since when do you know Drago Nikolic or when did you meet Drago Nikolic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: When I came to the brigade as a signalsman and started doing shifts at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you help us with a date or something, a time frame?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJKIC
utterances.text: No, I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I just take your answer, when did you -- when is it that you started to be signalsman at the IKM to do a shift? What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings your testimony to an end, Mr. Stojkic. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over and I also wish you on behalf of everyone a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exhibits? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have no exhibits with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No exhibits, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just that 3396, the tactical command with his name on it had not been in evidence before so we would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objections, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't suppose the other Defence teams have an interest in this so that document is admitted. All right. One moment, let's thrash the -- Mr. Sarapa, did you consult with Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did contact my colleagues from the Borovcanin Defence team, and since it is a witness, a joint witness, of their team and our Defence team, and we are just going to cross -- to examine him once, when he is called, and with respect to all the measures required we agree that it be in the manner in which the Borovcanin team has requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, 30 days before the beginning of the Borovcanin Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the agreement we reached during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's decide it here and now. So pursuant to Rule 75 and the Tribunal's jurisprudence, the Trial Chamber finds that the circumstances of Witnesses 7DW-14 and 7DW-12, also known as 4DW-16, warrant the provisional measures requested in the Pandurevic motion and the Borovcanin joining motion, and that their fear is objectively founded. The Trial Chamber therefore accedes to the request and grants the protective measures requested. The disclosure of the identity of Witness 7DW-14 will be made -- shall only be made 30 days prior to his respective anticipated date of testimony, while that of common Witness 7DW-12 and 4DW-16, the disclosure of his identity will be made 30 days prior to the commencement of the Borovcanin Defence case. Okay. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber I welcome you to this Tribunal and to this case. You are a Defence witness. You've been summoned by the Defence team for Colonel Vujadin Popovic. Sorry to have kept you waiting but we had another witness. You're going to start soon and then we continue tomorrow and hopefully finish. Before you start your testimony, you need to enter a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. That is the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that's your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Make yourself comfortable, please. Mr. Zivanovic, you go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Acimovic. I'd like to start off by introducing myself, although you know me already. But I'd like to do that officially, as is the rule here. My name is Zoran Zivanovic and in this case I'm Defence counsel for Vujadin Popovic. I'm going to ask you to state your name and surname for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you give us your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of November 1966 in Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the secondary school of traffic and I graduated from that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a traffic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me where you worked, in what company or institution.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the ZTO of Serbia. And my branch office was in Loznica and Novi Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what this abbreviation, ZTO, stands for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's the railways of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you ever mobilised and if so, when? When the war started in Bosnia? Or prior to the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised in March 1992, and in my military booklet, the date says from the 20th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me where you were mobilised at that time, in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised in the reserve force of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- well, when you say the Yugoslav Army, do you mean the JNA, the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, were you in the Army of Republika Srpska too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what unit you were in of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was in the military police, and later on, I went to Trsic company which held the line at Boskovici. And from there, I transferred to the signals company of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that throughout, you were within the composition of that particular brigade, the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who the commander of your signals company was while you were in it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: The signals company commander was Sergeant Dragisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his surname perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Radic, Dragisa Radic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was somebody who was the chief of signals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of signals was Captain Milosav Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which duties you performed in the signals unit you were in while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I worked on the switchboard, TC 10. Then I was transferred to help out the signalsmen up at the line, establishing lines with the battalions, and then I returned to the switchboard and worked at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you helped link up the battalions, can you tell us what you actually did, what was your job, what did it entail?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were wire connections, wire lines, which went up to the battalion, and it was our job to keep the line from the battalion, brigade, command to the battalion to keep the line open there. Now, the lines in the battalions themselves were maintained by the signalsmen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to stop here today. We will continue tomorrow, sir. And for the record, for this last part of the session, Mr. Vanderpuye and Ms. Janisiewicz were present. Thank you. Tomorrow we are sitting in the afternoon. Mr. Acimovic, I want to make sure you understand what I'm going to tell you. Between now and tomorrow when you continue and finish your testimony you're not to speak or communicate with anyone in relation to the subject matter that you're testifying upon. 25

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.
